Photograph: WWBT/AP View image in fullscreen Police investigate the scene of a shooting on the campus of Virginia State University on 15 August 2026. Photograph: WWBT/AP Virginia Multiple people injured in shooting at Virginia State University School said shooting involved ‘multiple suspects’ as campus was locked down and police responded to scene Adam Gabbatt Sat 15 Aug 2026 09.20 EDT Last modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 12.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Multiple people were injured in a shooting at Virginia State University (VSU), police said on Saturday morning, with several suspects still at large. The campus, about 20 miles (32km) south of Richmond, was on lockdown when police released initial details about the shooting. “A shooting occurred in the area of the Quad Annexes involving multiple victims, who were transported to area hospitals. Police are on scene and request that you avoid the area,” the VSU police department said in a statement . VSU said the shooting involved “multiple suspects”. Chesterfield county police, whose jurisdiction includes VSU, said officers discovered five people suffering from gunshot wounds outside campus dormitories when they arrived. The five victims were transported to hospitals, and one initially listed as having life-threatening injuries was later upgraded to critical condition, county police said. The other victims sustained non-life-threatening injuries, police said. Police told WTVR that police were called to university dormitories at 1.30am. The campus had a large law enforcement presence on Saturday morning. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) and the sheriff’s office of adjacent Hanover county were assisting, police said. As of Saturday morning, there had been nearly 300 mass shootings reported across the US so far for the year, according to the Gun Violence Archive . The nonpartisan resources defines mass shootings as cases in which at least four victims are wounded or killed. The US has perennially registered high numbers of mass shootings, with a considerable portion of those occurring at school and university campuses or activities. Those numbers have prompted calls for more substantial federal gun control, though Congress over the years has not implemented such restrictions. The shootings happened just before the start of the academic year at Virginia State. According to the university’s website, residence halls opened for students a week ago, and classes are set to begin on Monday. Many students had just completed the university’s “New Trojans Experience” for incoming students, an event alluding to the nickname for the school’s athletic teams. The public university has about 5,700 students, most of whom are undergraduates. VSU has grown in recent years while attempting to improve safety and retain its historic charm, according to Arthur Fridrich, the university’s former director of distance education, who lives near the campus and visits regularly. For VSU’s community, a shooting just as students return for classes is heartbreaking, he said. “To start a new year with this event is very tragic. It casts a shadow in the minds of all students,” he said. https://www.dw.com/en/russian-american-h.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JZg8 The proposed 'Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity' would follow the path of a former Soviet railway, near the border with Iran Image: Anthony Pizzoferrato/Middle East Images/picture alliance Advertisement Until recently, few people in the South Caucasus had heard of Konstantin Sokolov. Now the 52-year-old Russian-American businessman is at the center of new investment fund backed by US President Donald Trump . In mid-July, Sokolov — who emigrated from Russia to the US at age 21 and later founded the investment firm IJS Investments in Chicago — was appointed to head a new investment fund of the US State Department. The TRIPP+ EnterpriseFund, registered in the US as the Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund and launched with more than $200 million (about €172.5 million) in capital, is expected to invest in countries across the South Caucasus and Central Asia and help finance the large-scale TRIPP infrastructure project, also known as the "Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity." The "Trump Route" is a transit corridor that aims to connect Azerbaijan with its autonomous exclave of Nakhchivan through Armenian territory. The ambitious infrastructure project is part of a peace deal that Armenia and Azerbaijan signed in August 2025 with US mediation. In early June 2026, Washington and Yerevan signed a framework cooperation agreement for the project. Experts have said construction of the "Trump Route" fits Washington's strategy of creating a trade corridor between Europe and the region that bypasses existing routes through Russia and Iran . Sokolov buys up Russian assets in Armenia Long before he was appointed to head TRIPP+, Sokolov had already established a foothold in Armenia. In 2024, he acquired Viva Armenia, the country's largest telecommunications provider. Despite its subsequent partial nationalization, Sokolov continued to expand his holdings. Recently, his companies also bought up the Armenian subsidiary of Russian telecom giant Rostelecom. In August 2025, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev (left) and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan (right) signed a joint declaration 'peace road map' after talks with Trump Image: Azerbaijan Presidency/Anadolu/picture alliance An even more significant deal, however, was carried out largely out of the public eye: the purchase of the Teghut copper-molybdenum mine. The mine, which holds an estimated 450 million metric tons of ore and has Armenia's second-largest reserves, had been taken over by Russia's state-owned VTB Bank after the company accumulated massive debts. VTB is now under Western sanctions. According to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty's Armenian service, the deal was carried out through a third-party company. "Sokolov wanted to avoid a direct deal with the Russian bank," said Mkrtich Karapetyan, a Radio Liberty journalist who has been investigating the flow of foreign capital into Armenia. Sokolov: Trump supporter, MAGA backer While Armenia's government and its supporters have welcomed the influx of Western capital into the country's infrastructure projects, the opposition has highlighted serious risks. Mesrop Manukyan, a lawmaker from the opposition Armenia Alliance, is among Sokolov's most vocal critics in parliament. He said it's alarming that a US investor has been able to acquire major stakes in the finance, mining and telecommunications sectors in just a few years. Manukyan's faction, which advocates close ties between Armenia and Russia, opposes the TRIPP+ project. It views the "Trump Route" as a disguised "extraterritorial corridor" and the "greatest threat" to Armenia's security. Armenia looks to EU after decades of relying on Russia To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Despite his extensive investments, Sokolov remains largely unknown to the Armenian public. There are no official photos of him, and he generally avoids interviews with the local press during business trips. His most recent visit to the capital, Yerevan, was in early August, when he met with Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan. He was accompanied by Aryeh Lightstone, senior adviser to US special envoy Steve Witkoff. In Western media, however, Sokolov is known not only for his business ventures in the US and Switzerland but also for his political involvement. Sokolov is a major donor to the US Republican Party and a Trump supporter. According to The Associated Press, he donated about $11 million to Trump's MAGA movement over the course of a year. 'Compromise' between Moscow and Washington? Benyamin Poghosyan of the Armenian think tank APRI sees two main reasons for Sokolov's appointment to head the fund. The first is political. Appointing an American with Russian roots could be "a subtle gesture by Washington aimed at easing Moscow's fierce criticism of the project," he told DW. The second, however, is pragmatic. "Perhaps Russia has nothing to do with it at all. Sokolov may simply have been chosen because he has a deep understanding of the business environment in the former Soviet Union — and because he knows Armenia and how its government works," said Poghosyan. Armenia and Azerbaijan were locked in a conflict over the Nagorno-Karabakh region for decades Image: Tofik Babayev/AFP/Getty Images At the same time, the sheer scale of the investment and the financier's Russian roots are fueling speculation in Armenia. Social media users in the country are debating whether Sokolov, who was born in St. Petersburg, could be a secret "compromise figure" between Moscow and Washington. Supporters of the theory point to the ease with which US companies have acquired formerly Russian assets subject to Western sanctions. Other observers have refuted the idea, noting that Sokolov has publicly and sharply criticized the Russian government and its war against Ukraine . The funds provided by the US State Department, running through 2036, are seen as flagging Washington's long-term strategic intentions in the region. During his visit to Yerevan, Aryeh Lightstone told Armenian news outlet CivilNet that the more than $200 million in initial funding could be viewed as a starting point for future investments. Aram Sargsyan, head of the Republican Party of Armenia and an ally of Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, also rejects the idea that Sokolov is a "compromise figure" for Moscow. He emphasized the practical value of Sokolov's background, seeing it as an opportunity rather than a cause for concern. "Sokolov has significant business contacts, understands the Russian mentality perfectly, speaks the language and knows how to work with relevant Russian institutions," he said. This article was originally written in Russian. Europe Sweden Lowers Age of Criminal Responsibility to 14 The measure, aimed at gangs that recruit children too young to be prosecuted, passed with backing from the opposition Social Democrats. Save Mark Us Preferred on Google Print Members of Parliament arrive at Parliament in Stockholm on July 7, 2021. Christine Olsson/TT via AP Etienne Fauchaire 8/15/2026 | Updated: 8/16/2026 0:00 X 1 Sweden’s parliament voted on Aug. 13 to lower the age of criminal responsibility from 15 to 14 for the most serious offenses, opening the way for children of that age to be sentenced to prison. The Swedish reform passed by 281–66, with the progressive opposition Social Democrats siding with the minority conservative government of Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, who has vowed to crack down on crime, and its right-wing ally, the Sweden Democrats. The Left, Green, and Centre parties voted against the measure. Most provisions take effect on Sept. 10, three days before the country’s general election. For more than 10 years, the Scandinavian nation has been plagued by violent turf wars between rival gangs, driven largely by the fight over the drug trade. 5-Year Experiment Aimed at Gangs The lowered threshold covers only crimes carrying a minimum of four years in prison, such as murder, aggravated rape, kidnapping, and aggravated weapons offenses, and will lapse after five years unless lawmakers renew it after an evaluation. Related Stories Rising Violent and Property Crimes Fuel Spike in Youth Charges: StatCan He Survived a Bow-and-Arrow Attack, Now He’s Speaking Out Again After a Shopkeeper’s Death Fourteen-year-olds sentenced to prison will serve their terms in special youth units in prison. The government argued that criminal networks deliberately recruit children younger than 15 for shootings and bombings precisely because they cannot be punished and that suspects in fatal shootings keep getting younger: 52 children younger than 15 were involved in court proceedings over murders or murder plots last year, it stated. The government had initially sought to set the age at 13, but withdrew that bill in June for lack of a majority after most of the 126 groups consulted, including the police and the prison service, opposed it. The Children’s Ombudsman, Save the Children, UNICEF Sweden, and the state crime prevention council have opposed the age lowering, with several claiming that no research shows that it reduces offending and that the younger a child is prosecuted, the higher the risk of reoffending. Lawmakers also voted to scale back sentence reductions for young offenders, meaning that minors younger than 18 can now face prison terms of up to 18 years. A Broader European Shift For Frédéric Pichon, a French criminal defense lawyer, Sweden’s about-face tells the story of a continent. “[Nordic countries long pursued] extremely liberal policies, both on criminal matters, particularly toward minors, and on immigration,” he told The Epoch Times. “Today, they are confronted with the consequences of decades of ideological denial.” Europe in general, he said, faces the same reckoning: gravely violent cases involving minors have multiplied over the past years. Across Europe, governments confronted with ever younger and ever more violent offenders are hardening their juvenile justice systems. In France, Parliament adopted a law championed by former Prime Minister Gabriel Attal in May 2025 to toughen the treatment of juvenile offenders and their parents. The Constitutional Council struck down the law’s flagship provisions the following month, including an end to the reduced sentences for repeat offenders aged 16 and older, ruling that mitigated punishment based on a minor’s age is a constitutional requirement. In Germany, where the threshold has stood at 14 since 1923, senior Christian Democrats have called for lowering it to 12, and the governing coalition agreed in 2025 to commission a study on the question, although no change has been adopted. Hungary made 12-year-olds punishable for homicide and a few other grave crimes in 2013, provided that they understood their acts. Lowering the age nonetheless addresses only the end of the chain, Pichon said. “When a young person reaches 15 or 16, it is already too late,” he said. What society needs, Pichon said, is a restoration of the concept of authority along with greater parental responsibility and an end to the glorification of violence in popular culture. Photograph: National Parks Service/AP California Two helicopter pilots killed while battling Yosemite fires A helicopter assisting in fighting the Dome fire in Yosemite national park crashed on Sunday afternoon Maanvi Singh and agency Mon 21 Sep 2026 16.50 EDT Last modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 16.53 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Two helicopter pilots died while fighting a fire in Yosemite national park on Sunday afternoon. The pilots were conducting water drops over the Dome fire, which had burned more than 3,000 acres since it ignited last week, when their helicopter crashed around 3pm, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. ‘We’re near a breaking point:’ firefighters say US government is failing them amid intense wildfire season Read more The pilots were employed by the aerospace company Precision and were working with a wildland firefighting crew that specializes in using ropes to descend from helicopters to reach otherwise inaccessible terrain, known as helitack rappelling. The helicopter went down southeast of Ostrander Lake, said Benjamin Cossel, a spokesperson with the Federal Complex Incident Management Team overseeing the firefighting response. Details about the circumstances surrounding the crash were not immediately released. The crash will be investigated by the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transportation Safety Board. “It is with unimaginable sadness and broken hearts that we share the loss of two beloved members of our team,” Precision wrote in a social media post. “We are devastated by this loss and are struggling to find the words. We ask for privacy and compassion for their families and our team as we grieve this tremendous loss.” The names of the pilots were not immediately released. Roughly 580 people are fighting the Dome Fire, which started on 15 September near Wawona, California , according to the National Interagency Fire Center. It’s burning on about 4.7 sq miles (12.3 sq km) and is about 15% contained. The lake near the crash site was roughly 9 miles (14.5km) south of Yosemite’s iconic El Capitan, and about 7 miles (11.3km) northeast of Wawona. Water-dropping helicopters have been key to fighting the blaze, which has spread across rugged terrain. At least 14 people have died while helping with wildfires in the US this year, the most since 2022 when 25 deaths were recorded, according to government reports. Three firefighters died battling Colorado’s Knowles fire , and an additional member of that crew succumbed to injuries weeks afterwards. The incident was the most deadly entrapment in 13 years. The job has always carried inherent risks,but this year has been especially dangerous. The Trump administration has increased pressure on firefighting forces, amid a critical shortage of federal firefighters. RodrÃ­guez succeeded NicolÃ¡s Maduro shortly after US forces conducted a raid on the Venezuelan capital Caracas and seized him. The pair met a few kilometres from the New York jail where Maduro is awaiting trial for drug trafficking and other charges. RodrÃ­guez said they discussed "advancing a cooperation agenda in strategic areas such as energy, mining, and security". US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles also attended the meeting. RodrÃ­guez's government has signed an agreement allowing the US to control more than 65 billion barrels of its oil - more than a fifth of the country's reserves. It grants a US-led company 100-year concessions over 17 oilfields in Venezuela. Trump previously called it "the biggest oil deal in world history". During his address to the UN on Monday, Trump said the US and Venezuela control "more than 60%" of the world's oil, adding: "To the victor belong the spoils." RodrÃ­guez is due to address the UN on Wednesday. She previously served as vice-president to Maduro and was sanctioned by the US in 2018, but the measures were lifted in April this year. She was sworn in as interim president by Venezuela's National Assembly days after the US raid with the White House's blessing. Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado has repeatedly been barred from re-entering the country .
